note: Teaching metadata only. Verdicts are never stored here: the UI always shows the checker's live result. Regression expectations live in tests/fixtures/expected.json.

scenarios.title: Two threads share one counter
scenarios.lesson: A read and a write that are separate steps can be interleaved. The checker finds the schedule where both threads read 0 and the second write erases the first: a lost update.
scenarios.try: Open the broken model, run it, step the witness: A.read, B.read, A.write, B.write. Then open the repaired model, where increment is one atomic action.

scenarios.title: Two checkouts, one unit in stock
scenarios.lesson: Check-then-act: both workers see stock > 0 before either reserves. The fix is an atomic conditional update.
scenarios.try: Compare the two runs in the Witness Archive: the repaired graph has fewer reachable states and no scarlet node, because the transition relation changed.

scenarios.title: Concurrent transfers and conservation of money
scenarios.lesson: Two opposite transfers with split read/write steps can create or destroy money. With atomic debits and credits, money in flight is accounted for and conservation holds in every reachable state.
scenarios.try: Notice the repaired invariant is stronger: it must hold in every state, not only at the end.

scenarios.title: A lock built from a plain flag
scenarios.lesson: Checking a flag and setting it are two steps unless the hardware gives you test-and-set.
scenarios.try: Use the Interleaving Theater to advance one process at a time and build the violating schedule yourself.

scenarios.title: Two locks in opposite order
scenarios.lesson: A deadlock is a reachable state with no enabled action that is not an intended end state. A global lock order removes the circular wait.
scenarios.try: The deadlock witness is only two steps long. The repaired model has a terminal state, which is declared, so it is not a deadlock.

scenarios.title: At-least-once delivery and duplicate side effects
scenarios.lesson: A visibility timeout cannot tell a slow consumer from a dead one, so the message is redelivered and the side effect happens twice. Recording the message id atomically with the effect makes processing idempotent.
scenarios.try: Acceptance journey 3: run, read the duplicate-output witness, switch to the idempotent model, re-run.

scenarios.title: Bounded buffer: capacity and progress
scenarios.lesson: A missing full-check lets the buffer exceed its capacity. The repaired model also proves (in this finite model) that every item is eventually consumed under weak fairness.
scenarios.try: Look at the liveness row: it names the fairness assumptions it used.

scenarios.title: Why liveness needs fairness
scenarios.lesson: Reachability shows the count CAN reach 3. Liveness asks whether it MUST. Without fairness a behaviour may stop forever (stutter) at 0.
scenarios.try: The unfair witness is one initial state followed by 'stutter forever'.

scenarios.title: Starvation: weak versus strong fairness
scenarios.lesson: B's acquire is enabled only while the lock is free, so it is not continuously enabled. Weak fairness cannot force it; strong fairness can. Fairness changes the verdict only when it is encoded on the right action.
scenarios.try: Open all three variants. The no-fairness and weak-fairness witnesses differ: one stutters, one cycles.

scenarios.title: Livelock versus Peterson's algorithm
scenarios.lesson: In a livelock every step makes 'progress' and the scheduler is fair, yet nobody enters. Peterson's turn variable breaks the symmetry.
scenarios.try: The livelock witness is a cycle (shown in the condensed SCC view); every fairness constraint is satisfied on the loop.

scenarios.title: Leader leases and fencing tokens
scenarios.lesson: A lease that expires while its holder is paused produces two writers who both believe they lead. Storage-side fencing with monotonically increasing tokens rejects the stale one.
scenarios.try: Find the expire step in the witness: nothing tells N1 its lease ended.

scenarios.title: Reordered messages
scenarios.lesson: Reordering is modelled as a nondeterministic choice of which in-flight message the network delivers next, never as a UI animation.
scenarios.try: Compare the two witnesses' Network lane.

scenarios.title: Cache-aside and the stale refill
scenarios.lesson: A reader that fills the cache after a writer invalidated it puts stale data back. A version check on fill drops the stale value.
scenarios.try: Step the witness; the stale read is the miss before the update.

scenarios.title: Retries and duplicate authorization
scenarios.lesson: A lost reply plus a client retry produces a second charge. An idempotency key stored with the result makes retries safe.
scenarios.try: The Network lane drops a reply; nothing else is fake.

scenarios.title: Two-phase commit: presume commit or presume abort
scenarios.lesson: Treating a missing vote as yes breaks atomic commitment. Presuming abort is safe in this model, at the price of aborting more often.
scenarios.try: Two invariants fail in the broken model; their witnesses have different lengths.

scenarios.title: Three dining philosophers
scenarios.lesson: A symmetric protocol can deadlock; reversing one philosopher's fork order removes the cycle in the wait-for graph.
scenarios.try: The deadlock witness takes three steps: every philosopher holds one fork.

scenarios.title: State explosion and honest INCOMPLETE
scenarios.lesson: Three independent counters already give 1,000 states. With a 50-state cap the verdict is INCOMPLETE, never 'safe'.
scenarios.try: Acceptance journey 6: set Max states to 50, run, export the receipt, tamper with it, verify.
